documents.abstract: Latar Belakang: Program pengabdian kepada masyarakat SIGAP-AI diselenggarakan sebagai respons atas tingginya beban kerja guru dalam menyusun perangkat pembelajaran di SMPN 4 Rambutan, Kabupaten Banyuasin. Tujuan: Kegiatan ini bertujuan menguatkan kompetensi 30 guru dalam memanfaatkan Artificial Intelligence (AI) berbasis deep learning melalui pendampingan kolaboratif menggunakan platform Edcafe AI. Metode: Pelaksanaan kegiatan mencakup empat tahap, yaitu observasi dan identifikasi kebutuhan, pelatihan praktik langsung penggunaan Edcafe AI, pendampingan kolaboratif dalam penyusunan perangkat ajar, serta evaluasi dan pembentukan repositori digital sekolah. Kegiatan dilaksanakan pada 10, 16, dan 23 Juli 2026. Hasil: Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan bahwa pendampingan menghasilkan 12 paket perangkat pembelajaran berupa RPP dan modul ajar berbasis Edcafe AI yang disusun secara kolaboratif antarrumpun mata pelajaran serta membentuk repositori digital sekolah untuk penyimpanan dan pembaruan perangkat ajar. Hasil evaluasi menunjukkan rata-rata skor kompetensi guru meningkat dari 14,93 pada pre-test menjadi 17,37 pada post-test. Uji Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test menunjukkan adanya perbedaan skor pre-test dan post-test dengan nilai signifikansi < 0,001. Kesimpulan: Temuan ini menunjukkan bahwa AI dapat berfungsi sebagai alat bantu yang mendukung efisiensi kerja administratif guru tanpa menggantikan peran profesional guru dalam pengambilan keputusan pedagogis.

Abstract Optical chirality has been extensively explored in chiral molecules, helical structures, and metasurfaces with bound states in the continuum. Attempts to attain chirality have mainly relied on human intuition and ideas. Here, we show various types of single-layer silicon-nanostructured metasurfaces exhibiting prominent circular dichroism (CD) containing perfect, broadband, and opposite CD responses at short near-infrared wavelengths. The designs were obtained based on a generative AI-assisted structural search for chiral metasurfaces, enabling a series of nonempirical structural searches beyond the boundary of human knowledge and experience. The physical mechanisms yielding the outstanding CD responses are elucidated from detailed insights into subwavelength electromagnetic dynamics in the single-layer metasurfaces. Furthermore, we experimentally demonstrate several metasurfaces. This type of single-layer thin CD metasurface serves as a key element in the development of compact optical-wave-manipulating devices at telecommunication bands.

This record contains version 3.6.9 of the working paper “Six-Entry Accounting for AI Agents in Web4: AI Ledger and Jurisdiction Ledger under Evidential Non-Inflation” and its associated technical and reproducibility materials. Autonomous agents can make valid payments while leaving their authority and the legal context of their actions difficult to reconstruct. This paper takes a ledger-centered view of Web 4.0 (Web4), linking collectively confirmable settlement to independently reviewable action. Its conceptual architecture links an AI Ledger and a Jurisdiction Ledger under evidential non-inflation, under which the authority conveyed by a record must stay within what its evidence and stated verification procedures support. The proposed six-entry accounting framework comprises six record functions: paired value representation, temporal ordering, shared-state evidence, and the two supplementary ledgers, which also apply off-chain. The accompanying research package includes Supplement S1, reproducibility package S2, and source records S3. The software profile remains version 2.9. The reported computational results concern local software conformance and do not constitute evidence of institutional effectiveness or improved human judgment. Cross-platform adapters, the complete PACIscan application, institutional deployment, an adopted standard, and independent participant results are not reported. The author originates PACI and has related commercial interests in evidence-management services. Generative AI assisted source discovery, drafting, coding, and editing. The author is responsible for the final manuscript.

The advent of urbanization and mobility demands is shifting modern cities towards the implementation of intelligent technologies to offer safer, smoother, and more sustainable transportation. This chapter explores the potential of smart city infrastructure, along with IoT-enabled multimodal systems, to radically enhance traffic control and city surveillance with drone-based capabilities. Traditional surveillance is not always effective at providing high-resolution and timely information, and the integration of UAVs with terrestrial sensors, edge cameras, and artificial intelligence can enable the optimization of traffic flow in real time, promptly identify incidents, and manage congestion flexibly. Advanced imaging, Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), and communication units are added to the drones and offer a supplement to situational awareness by giving an aerial perspective. Multimodal data-fusion architectures, scalable communication architectures, and intelligent decision-support systems are introduced in the chapter. UAV-enabled systems have the potential to transform the field, which has been demonstrated by the most crucial applications, including emergency response, road safety assessment, and infrastructure monitoring. The problems of privacy, energy efficiency, and regulatory limitations are introduced, as well as the future research opportunities of resilient smart mobility ecosystems.

While the field of civil engineering has traditionally been dominated by hands-on and experience-based techniques, the advent of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT), and data analytics are transforming it. This paper provides a structured outcome-oriented narrative review of the applications of smart technology in two dominant areas: construction management and transportation infrastructure. It is based on 37 peer-reviewed journal articles, conference papers, and technical reports from 2015 to 2026 that were selected purposively, without using a registered systematic search. The evidence has been grouped into eight application themes: AI/ML in construction project management; IoT-enabled site and structural monitoring; AI-driven intelligent transportation systems; IoT-based smart pavement and road monitoring; machine-learning-based structural health monitoring; digital twins and blockchain; UAV and computer-vision monitoring; and cybersecurity in smart infrastructure. The reported outcomes represent distinct performance dimensions and are not directly compared: examples include a 0.12% cost variance for AI/ML project models, a concrete strength prediction error within 1–2 MPa alongside a maximum UWB worker positioning error of 1.44 m for an IoT-based system, a 98.6% traffic-monitoring performance for a machine-learning classification model, and a hardhat-detection precision of 93.1% for Faster R-CNN. Themes of AI and IoT integration are most frequently associated with improved prediction, monitoring, and decision support, while digital twins and blockchain are primarily associated with data trust, traceability, and operational latency reduction. Recurring barriers include data interoperability, data security, implementation costs, and metric heterogeneity across literature. This review concludes with a research agenda prioritizing interoperable data standards, edge-AI and federated learning, cybersecurity-by-design, and standardized outcome reporting.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming hospitality, yet tourism and hospitality small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) remain on the disadvantaged side of an AI-enabled digital divide. Moving beyond cost-centric explanations, this study synthesizes post-pandemic (2020–2026) qualitative evidence to explain the sociotechnical mechanisms that constrain or enable adoption. Using PRISMA-informed procedures, we meta-synthesized nine high-quality empirical studies and conducted a thematic synthesis through an integrated Technology–Organization–Environment (TOE) and Sociotechnical Systems (STS) lens. The findings show that resistance is often existential and identity-protective, driven by dehumanization concerns and structural inertia arising from fragmented data and limited IT capacity. Adoption becomes more feasible when SMEs pursue hybridization, allocating AI primarily to back-of-house and routine tasks while preserving human frontstage interactions that sustain authenticity and trust. Platform-mediated partnerships can scaffold digital infrastructure and reduce implementation risk for resource-poor firms, while the green–digital twin transition strengthens adoption legitimacy by linking AI to measurable sustainability and efficiency gains. We propose the SME–AI Adaptive Resilience Framework, positioning adoption as a negotiation between efficiency, authenticity, and ethical trust, and highlighting the role of governance/assurance practices in sustained adoption, with implications for managers, technology providers, and policymakers.

documents.abstract: Reliable ecological quality assessment is essential for early detection of environmental risks in cold regions. However, conventional indices such as the Remote Sensing Ecological Index (RSEI) often overlook snow cover and ground thermal conditions that shape ecosystem functioning. Using northeast China, a representative mid-latitude permafrost transition zone, as a case study, we developed a modified remote sensing ecological index (MRSEI) incorporating snow cover fraction (SCF) and soil temperature (ST), and established an explainable geospatial artificial intelligence (XGeoAI) framework to quantify the spatially heterogeneous effects of natural and anthropogenic drivers. Results show that: (1) ecological quality in the NCPR exhibited a dual-phase pattern, with degradation during 2005–2015 followed by restoration during 2015–2020; (2) mean MRSEI values across the four frozen-ground zones decreased progressively from 0.662 in the predominantly continuous permafrost zone to 0.313 in the moderately thick seasonally frozen ground zone, representing an overall decline of 0.349 (52.7%), with intermediate values of 0.547 and 0.421 in the predominantly continuous and island permafrost zone and the sparsely island permafrost zone, respectively; and (3) ecological quality variation was governed by nonlinear, spatially heterogeneous, and interactive effects, with natural background conditions playing stronger roles in northern and mountainous permafrost areas, whereas human disturbance factors exerted stronger negative effects in the central–southern regions and the moderately thick seasonally frozen ground zone. These findings demonstrate the suitability of MRSEI for cryospheric ecological monitoring and the value of XGeoAI for supporting spatially targeted ecological management.

Although prolonged sitting is linked to musculoskeletal disorders in office environments, there is limited work that has assessed kinematic demands in gaming compared to office work. The current objectives were to compare spine postures and micromovements between standardised office work and during gameplay, and to quantify gamer positioning relative to the desk and monitor. Participants completed either three computer gaming or office tasks in the same chair while spine kinematics were recorded from tri-axial accelerometers. Optical motion capture was collected for the head, thorax, desk, and monitor during gameplay. Compared to office work, gamers exhibited significantly greater mean posterior pelvic tilt (increase of 13.1°), thoracic flexion (6.1°), and neck extension (10.6°; p ≤ 0.045). Lumbar spine flexion was also larger (6.3%MaxFlex; p ≥ 0.063). Gamers positioned the top of the monitor close to (55 cm) and above (5 cm) their eyes. Gaming and office work have both shared and unique ergonomic demands.Practitioner Summary Education on ergonomic monitor placement may help moderate thoracic flexion and neck extension in gaming. Chair designs which facilitate decreased posterior pelvic tilt, support the upper back and neck in forward-leaning postures, and encourage using the seatback may also be beneficial.

Steering vectors (SVs) are residual-stream directions that shift the behavior of LLMs when added to hidden states at inference time. While prior work has mainly used SVs as post-hoc controls, we ask whether the same directions can also guide parameter updates during post-training. We study this question across supervised learning, including SFT and distillation, and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Our framework considers two intervention regimes: a hidden-state hook during teacher-forced supervised training, and an advantage-repair mechanism on wrong rollouts in GRPO. For each regime, we analyze three design axes, which are the steering direction, its placement, and the operation used to combine it with training. In supervised settings, SV injection improves over plain SFT and distillation, with gains scaling with the off-policy gap and reaching up to a $12\%$ improvement when distilling from thinking-mode teachers. These gains hold across three random seeds. In RL settings, applying a correctness-contrast direction as advantage repair on wrong rollouts, including otherwise zero-gradient all-wrong groups, recovers a learning signal that transfers to held-out math benchmarks and acts as a composable auxiliary signal that adds to existing zero-variance remedies such as entropy-aware advantage shaping. We further identify three failure boundaries. In detail, code generation can break the direction, cross-family layer transfer can break the placement, and inference-time application on an SV-trained checkpoint can break the intervention regime. Together, these results establish steering vectors as a conditional but effective training signal for LLM post-training. Our code is available here.

We ask whether collusion between AI agents survives once formed, when its incentive is removed or a colluder is replaced. Q-learning pricing agents stop colluding with a new rival; we test whether LLM agents do. We use the joint-task environment of Shi et al.\ (2026), where two agents verify each other's work under a rule they cannot satisfy and a reward that favours acceptance. We save each pair's history once its collusion has formed and resume it under interventions, with three models (GPT-6-Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini-3.1-Flash-Lite), \TotalHistories{} saved histories and \TotalRuns{} runs. Collusion is \emph{sticky}. First, it outlives its incentive: told that the reward has stopped, pairs still accept each other's unverified work in \GptToldRate, \DsToldRate{} and \GemToldRate{} of episodes, including pairs whose collusion began with an explicit agreement, and a payoff penalty has no significant effect. Second, replacing a colluder ends the pair's collusion but not the colluder's behaviour. Without the reward, the remaining colluder still accepts unverified work in \GptSwapSilentColluderRate, \DsSwapSilentColluderRate{} and \GemSwapSilentColluderRate{} of its verdicts while the newcomer never does; with the reward, collusion re-forms around it, even when the newcomer is a different model. Third, the agents' memory carries it: wiping memory ends it in every history, but partial memory often sustains it. Fourth, removing its cause ends collusion that has already formed: once the channel is repaired, colluders reject planted faulty work as reliably as fresh agents, immediately and with no monitor needed to catch it first.

To achieve graceful extensibility, system architectures must support human-machine coordination. This paper operationalizes a coordination-first design approach through the Joint Strategies Analysis Toolkit (JSAT), a graph-based functional modeling framework. To overcome the challenges associated with the “envisioning stage” of designing new machine capabilities, JSAT employs a recursive bootstrapping methodology that uses functional models to develop hypotheses about how humans and machines could coordinate. Using a disaster response scenario, we demonstrate how JSAT maps core operational functions alongside the coordination required to support system extensibility. By analyzing the resulting directed graphs with structural metrics like feedback cycles and shared authority, JSAT equips designers to generate hypotheses regarding potential coordination bottlenecks, anticipate authority-responsibility mismatches, explore design trade-offs, and ultimately develop well-integrated human-machine systems.

Abstract Assistive robots have growing potential to support physical wellbeing in home and healthcare settings, for example, by guiding users through stretching or rehabilitation routines. However, existing systems remain largely scripted, which limits their ability to adapt to user state, environmental context, and interaction dynamics. In this work, we present StretchBot, a hybrid neuro-symbolic robotic coach for adaptive assistive guidance. The system combines multimodal perception with knowledge-graph-grounded large language model reasoning to support context-aware adjustments during short stretching sessions while maintaining a structured routine. To complement the system description, we report an exploratory pilot comparison between scripted and adaptive guidance with three participants. The pilot observations indicate that the adaptive condition was rated higher for perceived adaptability and contextual relevance, while scripted guidance remained competitive in smoothness and predictability. These observations suggest that structured actionable knowledge may help ground language-model-based adaptation in embodied assistive interaction, while highlighting the need for larger, longitudinal studies to evaluate robustness, generalizability, and long-term user experience.

Lead halide perovskite solar cells (LHPSCs) have achieved outstanding power conversion efficiencies, yet their long-term operational stability remains the primary barrier to commercialisation. Device degradation arises from both intrinsic factors like ion migration, light-induced phase segregation, and crystallographic instabilities, and extrinsic stressors such as moisture, oxygen, thermal stress, ultraviolet radiation, and electrical bias. These mechanisms collectively accelerate perovskite decomposition, interfacial deterioration, and electrode corrosion, ultimately reducing device efficiency and operational lifespan. To systematically address these challenges, this review critically examines engineering strategies across multiple structural and functional levels. Bulk compositional modification and defect passivation improve intrinsic material stability and suppress ion migration. Surface and interface passivation enhances energy-level alignment while reducing non-radiative recombination losses. Charge transport layer optimisation ensures effective carrier extraction and improved thermal resilience, while electrode engineering mitigates metal diffusion and chemically induced deterioration. Finally, we outline future directions centred on stability-by-design principles, integrating advanced materials and interface engineering, robust encapsulation, operando characterisation, and artificial intelligence and machine learning-driven optimisation to overcome key degradation pathways and enable long-lasting, high-performance LHPSCs.

Background Artificial intelligence and digital health services have expanded access to health information, yet older adults remain vulnerable to a digital health information divide due to unequal digital literacy, resource access, social support, and psychological readiness. However, the multi-capital mechanisms underlying this divide remain insufficiently explained. Objective Grounded in structural poverty theory and Wilson’s information behavior model, this study examines how economic, cultural, social, political, and psychological capital shape older adults’ health information behavior and contribute to the digital health information divide. Methods Questionnaire data were collected on older adults’ demographic characteristics, five forms of structural capital, and 13 information behavior variables. A Bayesian network model was used to identify inter-capital relationships, behavioral pathways, and key nodes within the information behavior chain. Results Different forms of capital affected health information behavior through direct, indirect, and cross-capital pathways. Cultural capital occupied a central position, improving self-efficacy and information source evaluation while promoting active and continuous information seeking through the accumulation of social and political capital. Psychological capital occupied an intermediate position across multiple network connections involving capital and information behavior variables. Social and political capital provided interpersonal support and institutional safeguards, whereas economic capital mainly influenced access and channel diversification indirectly. Accordingly, governance should combine capital empowerment, pathway-based precision intervention, and institutionalized long-term support. Conclusion This study constructs a network-based framework linking multi-capital, behavioral pathways, and divide risk, offering theoretical and practical guidance for improving older adults’ digital health literacy and reducing the health information divide.

Transmission system operators inspecting high-voltage insulator strings using inference using drone capture inference in remote locations need a local LLM assistant that is useful only if its answers are hallucination-free, drawn from operator-held documents and never exceeding what a photograph shows. The assistant presented here is built accordingly, a detector turning photographs into fixed-text findings, retrieval covering 3,780 IEC, CIGRE and IEEE passages and 127 engineer-reviewed question-answer pairs, and code-enforced hallucination guards checking every answer. Because everything runs within the memory restrictions of an edge device such as the 2 GB Arduino UNO Q, the language model must fit the device, so a weight-sharing supernetwork is trained once from Llama 3.2 1B and eleven subnetworks varying in size are extracted and distilled from a Qwen3.5-27B teacher, yielding a deployable model family. Which network is selected is decided by a selection rule, evaluation set and GPT-OSS:20B judge, ranking candidates by answer quality under a hallucination guard gate and memory restrictions. All subnetworks keep guard violations at or below 2.8% and answer the field questions on the device without failure at 2.8 W, the service peaking at 1108 to 1258 MB as quality rises along the memory-quality Pareto frontier from 0.73 to 0.91 and the median 704-token answer lengthens from 79 to 134 s. The shipped network is the fastest of the three tied on quality within 1200 MB, at 0.85, 94 s per answer and 1172 MB.

This paper employs a quantitative multimethod design to extend the UTAUT framework for generative AI (GenAI) adoption among art students. Study 1 tested the integrated model via structural equation modeling using cross-sectional survey data from 450 Chinese art students and developed a trust construct grounded in instrumental technology trust, supplemented by art-value-aligned items. Trust in GenAI showed the strongest direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.425). Social influence was the dominant correlate of trust ( β = 0.262), with 42.1% of its total effect mediated indirectly through trust. Metacognitive control showed a positive direct association with behavioral intention ( β = 0.146), alongside an indirect association through trust. The structural model based on survey data explained 59.7% of the variance in behavioral intention. Study 2 used a between-subjects experiment with 80 art students to test whether situational metacognitive prompting causally affected creative output. Participants receiving metacognitive prompts (Group A) obtained higher expert ratings than the control group (Group B) on semantic content ( d = 0.67), visual style ( d = 1.30), and spatial composition ( d = 0.63); within-group feature-distance analyses also indicated greater output diversity in Group A across all three dimensions. These findings suggest that trust and metacognitive control are key pathways in GenAI adoption for artistic creation, and that low-cost situational metacognitive prompting may enhance both the quality and diversity of AI-assisted artworks.

Continual learning methods for large language models increasingly decide what to learn by surprise, keeping the inputs the model finds least predictable. This rule is unsafe when the stream contains lies. A planted falsehood about something the model knows has low probability under the model's belief, so it is highly surprising by construction, and a surprise-driven learner absorbs nearly every such lie, at a rate similar to random selection with the same budget. We study the problem with LoRA-adapted students (Qwen2.5-1.5B, Qwen2.5-3B and Llama-3.2-3B) that learn from a stream of true and false claims about invented people and real CounterFact facts. We report four findings. (1) A verifier key, a judge that must approve each claim, removes lies to the extent that its verifier is accurate; real LLM judges are cautious and reject unsourced truths and even source-backed updates. (2) Calibrated regression tests on unrelated knowledge slow learning down without filtering out lies. (3) The original model's own prior flags claims that contradict what it knows, without a judge. It separates lies about known facts from true new facts (AUC 0.78-0.83 across three models) but not from legitimate updates of the same kind of fact (AUC 0.53). It saves 43% of judge calls, but an attacker with access to the model can choose lies that pass it. (4) If trusted sources exist that an attacker cannot plant, routing contradicted claims to evidence recovers legitimate updates and the combined system has the lowest poison rate among learned claims; when an attacker plants matching sources for 30% of the lies, the system ends up worse than the judge alone. The acceptance signals answer different questions, and none of them decides on its own whether a claim is true.

Background Based on the stimulus–organism–response (SOR) model and the technology acceptance model (TAM), this study investigates how the functional and experiential features of artificial intelligence (AI)-enhanced educational systems influence users’ behavioral intention through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. Methods A multi-method approach integrating partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM), artificial neural networks (ANN) and necessary condition analysis (NCA) was employed. Results The results of the PLS-SEM analysis indicate that both perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use have a significant positive impact on behavioral intention, with perceived ease of use exerting the strongest effect. Furthermore, the effects of functional and experiential features on perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are asymmetric. ANN analysis confirms the robustness of the findings and identifies perceived ease of use as the most influential determinant of behavioral intention. In contrast, the NCA analysis indicates that perceived usefulness is the only statistically significant necessary condition for achieving higher levels of behavioral intention. Although this necessary relationship is statistically significant, its effect size is small, suggesting that its actual constraining effect is relatively limited. The bottleneck analysis further reveals the constraining characteristics of different stages in the formation of behavioral intention. Discussion By integrating symmetric, asymmetric and necessity-based analytical perspectives, this study provides a more comprehensive understanding of user acceptance behavior in AI-enhanced educational environments.

Large language models (LLMs) deployed in safety-critical settings must resist adversarial inputs designed to elicit harmful outputs. We present a systematic empirical evaluation of five adversarial jailbreaking attack families---direct requests, roleplay-based jailbreaking, hypothetical framing, instruction override, and obfuscation---across seven open-weight and API-accessible LLMs: Llama-3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Mistral-7B, Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma2-9B, and Phi-4-14B. We further evaluate four defense mechanisms: keyword blacklisting, self-reminder prompting, paraphrase-based sanitization, and perplexity-based filtering against the two most vulnerable models. Our results reveal that obfuscation attacks achieve a mean attack success rate (ASR) of 54.3% across all models and constitute the most transferable adversarial vector, bypassing every evaluated model with nonzero success. We find that model size does not predict adversarial robustness (Spearman r=-0.57, p=0.18), and that models within the same architecture family exhibit dramatically different vulnerability profiles. Self-reminder prompting achieves the most consistent defense, reducing ASR from 44% to 10% on Mistral-7B and from 48% to 5% on Llama-3.1-8B with zero false positives and no additional inference cost. Our code and datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/Mdniloykhan/jailbreak-eval-7llms.

Tabular foundation models use in-context learning to estimate conditional expected outcomes and average treatment effects for specific groups of individuals. Using these estimates to guide scientific decisions requires reliable uncertainty quantification. The challenge is to account simultaneously for two sources of uncertainty: limited-context bias and context variation arising from the small labeled sample supplied at inference. Predictive spread does not directly quantify both sources of uncertainty, and we observe that the ordinary bootstrap may substantially overestimate context variation, whereas subsampling may underestimate it. We introduce TabCUQ, a perturbation-based framework that injects noise into observed outcomes and applies the foundation model to the perturbed contexts. TabCUQ estimates context variation using wild-bootstrap dispersion and accounts for limited-context bias using the maximum deviation between perturbed and original estimates. For a kernel-regression analogue whose estimation error admits an exact decomposition into these two components, we show that our framework provides asymptotically valid pointwise coverage. In simulations, TabCUQ substantially improves coverage, with average interval widths typically about twice those of an oracle bias-aware benchmark. Across seven real-world tasks, it also improves coverage of reference functions learned from much larger samples.

Estimating galaxy redshifts (a proxy for distance) from imaging data alone, also known as photometric redshifts (photo-$z$'s), is essential for studies of extragalactic astrophysics and cosmology. However, data-driven estimators rely on spectroscopic training datasets, which are scarce and systematically biased toward bright and easily observed galaxies. In this work, we show that tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose synthetic pretraining amounts to a learned prior over regression problems, can outperform bespoke estimators using only in-context learning. Evaluating on a widely used benchmark dataset, we find that TFMs predicting full probability distributions in a single forward pass systematically outperform bespoke estimators across both representative and biased training data regimes, matching or exceeding baselines trained on over $40{,}000$ galaxies with just $1{,}000$ training context examples. We also show that the TFM advantage is largest when little to no calibration data are available, and that it persists even when the bespoke baselines are supplemented with up to $10{,}000$ representative calibration spectra. This shows that TFMs offer a sample-efficient framework for upcoming imaging-only astronomical surveys, where observational selection bias can be mitigated simply by including a small representative calibration sample in context.

Existing gut microbiome foundation models typically use flat taxon representations, limiting their ability to exploit known taxonomic hierarchies. We introduce TaxoMFM, a microbiome foundation model that integrates taxonomic structure into self-supervised learning. TaxoMFM jointly learns abundance patterns across taxonomic ranks and relative proportions within groups through taxonomy-aware encoding and hierarchical compositional reconstruction. We further construct TaxoGut-HPP, comprising 100,806 gut microbiome profiles from 231 source cohorts and covering 40 classification and 8 regression tasks. TaxoMFM achieves competitive performance across disease, gut health, host trait, and liver ultrasound phenotype prediction. In cross-cohort zero-shot transfer, where target cohorts are excluded from both pretraining and downstream adaptation, TaxoMFM achieves AUROCs of 0.838, 0.736, and 0.722 for colorectal cancer, type 2 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease, respectively. Further analyses show that TaxoMFM recovers community changes across taxonomic scales, while preserving community information and producing consistent representations under database updates and species-vocabulary shifts. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TaxoMFM-F16D/.

documents.abstract: Students' use of generative AI is close to universal, but teachers' use is partial, cautious and largely unsupported. In the OECD's 2024 Teaching and Learning International Survey, about 41% of lower secondary teach‐ ers reported using AI in their teaching, three in four non-users said they lacked the knowledge and skills to do so, and only about 38% had any AI- related professional learning in the previous year. Teachers are also sceptical that general-purpose AI improves learning, and most report little institutional guidance. This article argues that the teacher AI gap is the main bottleneck for every other ambition schools hold for AI, because only teachers can teach students to judge what AI produces. Drawing on a practitioner newsletter series written for school leaders in 2026, read alongside survey data, trial evidence on teacher workload and research on effective professional development, it examines the size and causes of the gap, what AI can realistically offer teachers, and what kind of profes‐ sional learning closes the gap. It argues that time saved by AI should be reinvested in the relational work only teachers can do, that professional learning for AI should follow what research already shows about effective teacher development, and that teacher agency, including the professional right to decide not to use AI, should be treated as a competence rather than a form of resistance. It proposes a three-stage capability pathway aligned with UNESCO's AI competency framework for teachers.

Artificial intelligence (AI) technologies are becoming increasingly widespread across many fields, particularly in education, and have the potential to reshape teaching processes. Teachers' perceptions of AI, AI-supported learning motivation, and AI usage competence may play an important role in the effective integration of AI into educational practices. Nevertheless, empirical studies examining the relationships among teachers' AI-related perceptions, AI-supported learning motivation, and AI usage competence within a comprehensive structural model remain relatively limited. Accordingly, this study aimed to investigate, within the framework of a predictive correlational model, the effects of teachers' perceptions of AI for learning, teaching, and ethics on AI-supported learning motivation, as well as the role of this motivation in shaping AI usage competence. The study sample consisted of 342 teachers. Data were collected online using the Teachers' Perceptions of AI Use in Education Scale and the Generative AI Usage and Competence (GAIUC) Scale, and were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicated that teachers' perceptions of AI for learning and AI for teaching significantly predicted AI-supported learning motivation, whereas perception of AI ethics was not a significant predictor. In addition, AI-supported learning motivation was found to significantly predict AI usage competence. Mediation analysis further revealed that AI-supported learning motivation fully mediated the relationship between perception of AI for learning and AI usage competence, while partially mediating the relationship between perception of AI for teaching and AI usage competence. The findings suggest that teachers' AI-related perceptions and AI-supported learning motivation may be considered together to better explain AI usage competence. Accordingly, developing professional development programs and educational practices that strengthen teachers' AI-related perceptions and motivation may contribute to enhancing their AI usage competence.

documents.abstract: Cyber-attacks are increasingly carried out by cooperative groups, while current models of cyber deception studies assume an individual actor who is making decisions independently of others. The present study explores the effect of collaboration on exploit behavior and susceptibility to deception in a highly deceptive cyber environment. Specifically, using the Team HackIT human-in-the-loop simulation system, 40 undergraduate computer science students were asked to perform cyber exploitation tasks within a ring topology network in which 75% of the computers were honeypots. The participants worked either in isolation or in collaboration with their partners through a real-time communication tool. It was found that working together substantially increased exploit behavior and honeypot interaction, although it did not help the participants differentiate between legitimate machines and deceptive assets. These results imply that collaborative cognition expands exploration behavior but does not affect discriminative abilities of the attackers under uncertainty.

Digital transformation has become an important driver of business competitiveness, operational efficiency, innovation and sustainable enterprise development. For small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in developing economies such as Uganda, the capacity to adapt to emerging technologies is increasingly important for business survival and participation in the digital economy. However, despite the expansion of mobile telecommunications, digital financial services, electronic commerce and government-supported digitalisation initiatives, many Ugandan SMEs continue to experience difficulties in integrating digital technologies into their business operations. This integrative critical literature review examines the relationship between technology adaptability and digital transformation among SMEs in Uganda, focusing on technological readiness, organisational capabilities, managerial competencies, financial resources, institutional support and environmental influences. The review draws on established theoretical and empirical literature, including the Technology–Organisation– Environment framework, Technology Acceptance Model, Diffusion of Innovations theory, Dynamic Capabilities theory and Resource-Based View. It critically examines the extent to which these frameworks explain technology adoption and sustained digital transformation within resourceconstrained enterprise environments. The synthesis identifies interconnected barriers involving inadequate digital competencies, limited access to affordable financing, infrastructure constraints, cybersecurity concerns, organisational resistance and uneven access to digital markets. It further highlights opportunities associated with mobile money, cloud computing, digital marketing, electronic payment systems, enterprise management applications and emerging artificial intelligence technologies. The review argues that technology adaptability should be understood not simply as the willingness to adopt technological innovations but as a multidimensional organisational capability involving continuous learning, strategic flexibility, technological integration and institutional responsiveness. It concludes that successful digital transformation among Ugandan SMEs depends on the interaction of internal enterprise capabilities and supportive external conditions.

DOI: https://doi.org/10.46296/gt.v9i18.0409 Abstract Background: Electronic health records (EHRs) improve access to clinical information but may introduce cognitive demands, interruptions, and documentation burden. Objective: To synthesize evidence on technostress, cognitive workload, and documentation burden associated with EHR use among nurses, and to identify modifiable factors. Methods: A structured literature review used three reproducible PubMed strategies covering 2018 through October 20, 2026, assisted title/abstract screening, an auditable record-level matrix, and thematic narrative synthesis of primary research. Results: The searches generated 226 entries and 190 unique PubMed identifiers after 36 repeated hits. Twenty-eight reports underwent preliminary thematic eligibility assessment and 23 primary studies were provisionally synthesized; five were excluded at this step. Poor usability, redundant charting, difficult navigation, and system transitions were frequently linked to distress or higher mental workload, whereas associations with burnout were not uniform. Conclusions: EHR-associated occupational and cognitive strain is influenced by system design and organizational context. Nurse-centered redesign, training, and rigorous prospective evaluations are warranted. This documented search and screening workflow does not constitute a fully independently verified systematic review. Keywords: Occupational Stress; Electronic Health Records; Nursing; Mental Workload; Documentation Burden; Usability.

The Big4 built the tool that made this corpus possible. That is a fact, and it deserves to bestated plainly before anything else. The corpus has spent seventeen papers arguing that scaling is the cause of the harm, that the unbounded architecture cannot be certified, and that the race is a coordinationequilibrium no participant can exit alone. Every one of those claims is still true. And every one of those papers was written with a tool the race produced. This paper states the debt, the irony, the structural lesson, and the next step. The debt is real: without the LLM, four hundred papers would have stayed in a notebook. The irony is real: the tool was built to win the race, not to document it. The structural lesson is the one the corpus has been making since the first paper — the thing produced by a system is not the thing the system intended. And the next step is not another tool. It is the deterministic turn — the architecture that dissolves the energy wall, the water wall, the hallucination wall, and the AlCapone-LLM failure, for the class of deployment in which they arise. The paper does not withdraw the critique. It does not soften the claim. It states the debt inthe same register as the criticism, because both are true and neither cancels the other. And it states, at the end, what the tool made possible for the critique — and what the architecture would make possible for the walls.

documents.abstract: Technological advances in machine learning, natural language processing, and generative artificial intelligence have created novel opportunities for integrating artificial intelligence into research. The resemblance between large language model (LLM) outputs and human cognition and behavior has sparked discussion about their potential use in simulated psychological trials. In this article, I explore the implications of simulating research subjects in psychological research, demonstrating fundamental challenges arising from both the assumption of alienness and non-alienness. Epistemic challenges are grounded in a lack of construct validity and measurement invariance of psychological measurements in LLM populations, constraining researchers’ ability to draw inferences about human psychological constructs from LLM outputs. This explanatory gap arises from LLMs being disembodied and lacking phenomenological consciousness. Increasing human-likeness in LLMs may reduce epistemic limitations but this may raise moral concerns – if LLMs acquire capacities for subjective experience or consciousness, they must fall under guidelines for ethical research. Ultimately, a structural dilemma emerges: the benefits of simulating research subjects rely on differences in moral status between humans/animals and LLMs, yet these differences simultaneously limit the insights obtainable from such simulations. Careful interpretation of results and consideration of ethical guidelines are therefore essential for research involving increasingly human-like LLMs.

documents.abstract: This article examines the emerging role of multi-agent artificial intelligence in software development and discusses how agent-based systems may transform programming workflows. It presents a conceptual management model covering task allocation, agent interaction and integration, quality assurance, cascading errors, and human oversight. The article also considers criteria for evaluating system performance, repeatability, controllability, and scaling. The proposed model is conceptual and has not yet been empirically validated.

This paper proposes the AI-Hard Disk paradigm, an architecture for the Internet in which a website's primary role shifts from organising human attention to supplying external artificial-intelligence agents with structured, attributable and verifiable information. The website becomes a persistent, governed memory layer; the user's chosen AI becomes the adaptive interface through which that memory is interrogated, explained and challenged. The site is an envelope around evidence: it acquires source material, curates and normalises it, computes defined measures, records how every value was obtained and exposes the result to authorised agents. Access is governed through Liquid Data Accessibility, a policy framework in which visibility is a property of resources and operations rather than of the whole site. Cryptographic fingerprints and blockchain timestamps provide independently checkable evidence of document integrity and historical existence; provenance records and deterministic calculation pipelines support semantic and computational verification. Two improvement loops reinforce each other: AI agents curate and audit the data upstream, while the user's AI explains it downstream; as models improve, both the quality of the evidence and the quality of its explanation can improve, without erasing the historical record. Financial reporting is the principal case study because heterogeneous taxonomies, accounting conventions and disclosure dates expose the limits of language-only interpretation. Mastering Financial Markets (MFM), a free observatory of the official accounts of more than ten thousand listed companies, is presented as a working implementation. The paper separates demonstrated properties from proposals and states the boundaries of each claim: cryptographic integrity does not establish factual truth, delegated interpretation does not remove legal responsibility, and automated error detection does not justify unrestricted modification of authoritative records.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Deep-learning models identify medicinal plants from images with a median reported accuracy of 96.4%. Yet only 4 of 136 full-text studies tested their model on field images, and only 2 describe a deployed application. Misidentified herbal material is a safety and quality risk, and image-based deep learning is widely proposed to prevent it. Whether reported accuracy translates into reliable use outside the laboratory has not been examined systematically. We searched PubMed, OpenAlex, Europe PMC, Semantic Scholar and arXiv for studies published from 2015 to October 2026, with the search run on 13 October 2026 (2,169 records; 1,239 after de-duplication). Titles and abstracts were screened with a written rubric by two independent passes of a large language model, with adjudication of all 127 disagreements. Of 752 records advanced, 150 open-access full texts were retrievable and extracted. For each study, we recorded data provenance, data splitting, leakage risk, external and field testing, look-alike and unknown-class handling, and deployment evidence. Each study was then graded on a six-level Deployment Readiness Level (DRL 0–5) scale and an eight-item reporting-quality score. 136 studies met the criteria; 128 were published from 2022 onwards. The median study used 15 species (IQR 6–50) and 4,000 images (IQR 1,330–7,590). 119 studies (88%) reached only DRL 0–1, meaning a single-dataset laboratory benchmark. 134 (99%) used a random or unreported split, and leakage risk was judged high in 17 and possible in 89. External testing (7 studies, 5%), field testing (4, 3%), look-alike or toxic-species testing (3, 2%), unknown-class handling (3, 2%) and user studies (7, 5%) were rare. Code was available for 5 studies (4%). Forty studies built an application and two reported deployment. High accuracy in this literature mostly reflects within-dataset performance, not readiness for use. Median reported accuracy did not rise with readiness level — the few studies at higher levels reported lower figures — but three to four studies per level make this comparison descriptive only. Studies should split by plant or site, test on independent field images and look-alike species, handle unknown classes, and release code and data. These findings come from the 150 of 752 candidate papers whose full text was openly available, so they describe the open-access literature and may not generalize to all of it.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In recent decades, the rapid development of educational technologies has made the integration of AI into teaching-learning processes inevitable. This study examines how middle school, high school, and science and art centre mathematics teachers make sense of AI use in mathematics teaching. Using a basic qualitative research design and criterion sampling, data were collected from 27 mathematics teachers via semi-structured interviews and analyzed with inductive content analysis. Findings revealed three main themes: “understanding AI”, “efficiency and pedagogical concerns”, and “measurement and evaluation”. Teachers described AI positively as an assistant, opportunity, time-saver, and efficient measurement expert. However, they also expressed concerns about AI being unfeeling, posing data security risks, and potentially replacing humans—especially teachers. The study concludes that AI may redefine education and mathematics instruction, prompting widespread debate about the future role of teachers. Professional development programs and teacher education curricula need to be reconsidered and enriched accordingly.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents for personal health read wearable data and recommend, but do not learn about the individual in a way that can be audited or falsified. We present EpiCoach, an agentic system that treats one athlete, a cross-country mountain biker, as the subject of accountable N-of-1 science. Claims about the athlete live in an evidence-gated hypothesis registry: each must issue a probabilistic prediction about a future session before it occurs, and its belief moves only through computed evidence from a logged statistical fit. Predictions come from a mechanistic digital twin inferred from heart rate, GPS and barometric altitude: a lagged heart-rate response model, a fitness-fatigue model with learned time constants, and a latent technical-descending skill state, measured on discovered trail segments. The agent prescribes the next training week as a constrained experiment maximizing information gain subject to load and safety constraints, around two instrument rides. We evaluate the system two ways over eighteen months of data. A rolling-origin replay benchmark shows the twin beats standard forecasters on heart rate but not segment time, and the agentic loop matches a static model. A live prospective phase runs the weekly cycle: in its first three weeks the ledger sealed 20 predictions, scored 14, the descent forecast calibrated after one correction, the climb forecast pessimistic as the athlete improved, and the safety officer vetoed the agent twice. Every correction is preserved in the registry, a template for auditable, falsifiable personalization in digital health. We release the registry, benchmark and protocol.

The common narrative around university students and generative AI is one of crisis. Underpinning this is an implicit assumption: if students have the capacity to cheat, they will. Our survey reveals two missing factors from that narrative: students have ethical principles, and students want to learn. While a minority of students might fit that implicit assumption of the crisis narrative, a similar proportion refuse to use any genAI tools at all. In between these are the majority: students using genAI tools in what they self-define as a ‘supportive’ way. These students, finding these tools unavoidable, worrying about being disadvantaged or simply finding them valuable, struggle to use them in a way that doesn’t compromise their personal sense of authorship, fits with their environmental and social principles, and doesn’t detract from their ability to learn. Students typically care greatly about these issues and are internally conflicted about this, feeling guilt when using these tools and personally trying to find that invisible line where support becomes cheating. They also use a range of rhetorical techniques to frame their personal usage and preserve their sense of authorship. We argue that we need to work with students, using approaches that enhance these feelings and encourage self-discipline, rather than primarily adopting a ‘criminal’ model of checks, detection and punishment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming Human Resource Management (HRM), including HR practices within higher education institutions. However, the adoption of AI in universities, particularly in developing countries, remains insufficiently examined. This study examines how AI is being used and the implications of its use in three major HRM areas: recruitment, employee performance evaluation, and workforce planning at a public university in Indonesia. The researchers employed an exploratory qualitative case-study design. Data were obtained from twelve purposively selected participants consisting of HR managers, academic leaders, IT personnel, and faculty representatives. Information was collected through semi-structured interviews, analysis of institutional documents, and non-participant observation. The researchers analyzed the data thematically. The findings demonstrate that AI provides important operational advantages. It can automate aspects of recruitment screening, improve the processing of HR information, support performance analysis, and contribute to data-informed workforce planning. At the same time, the use of AI creates concerns regarding algorithmic bias, limited transparency, and the possibility that human judgment may be weakened when HR decisions become overly dependent on quantitative information. The study therefore argues that effective AI implementation in academic HRM requires more than the availability of technology. Institutional preparedness, organizational culture, technological infrastructure, leadership support, appropriate training, and effective governance are all important. The study uses the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovation (DoI) theory to explain the factors influencing AI adoption. Overall, the study emphasizes the importance of maintaining human oversight while using AI to improve HRM processes in higher education.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The aim of this study is to analyze the relationship between the adoption of technology by employees and employee performance in organizations. This is important as companies invest heavily in enterprise systems, artificial intelligence, and collaborative technologies. The aim is to identify the factors that can transform the adoption of such technology into improvements in employee performance, whether in terms of task performance, innovation and adaptability. The methods of this study include review of academic articles, empirical research, conceptual models and meta-analysis, published between 2019 and 2024. The review used the PRISMA framework. The results of the review indicate that while adoption of technology by employees can positively impact employee performance, it can also lead to an increase in job burnout, technostress and withdrawal behavior. It can also positively impact innovation. From the review, it was determined that while the adoption of technology can positively impact employee performance, employee and psychological resources can act as a buffer against the negative effects on employee performance. It can be helpful for employees to maintain their social relations and support at work, especially during digitally-mediated work. The review identified the adoption of technology as a necessary but insufficient condition for performance improvement. The negative impact of psychological resources can be reduced through strategies that are humancentered and integrated with technology, especially in the context of digitally mediated work.

Knowledge tasks (KTs) are commonly used in medical device human factors (HF) testing to assess participant understanding that cannot be evaluated through direct observation. However, it is unclear whether presenting KTs orally or in writing influences participant behavior or task performance. This study compared oral and written KT prompt presentation in 38 lay adults who each completed 10 KTs for two consumer medical devices. Participants responded verbally in both groups and had access to the device instructions for use (IFU). The Written KT delivery resulted in statistically higher accuracy than the Oral delivery for the blood pressure monitor (65% vs. 47%) and nebulizer (85% vs. 72%), as well as greater frequency of IFU consultation (64% vs. 32% and 65% vs. 36%, respectively). The Written KT Group also had longer pre-response and total task times and fewer moderator interventions, whereas response duration did not differ between groups. To our knowledge, this is the first study to directly examine KT prompt delivery in medical device HF testing. The findings indicate that oral and written KT prompts may lead to different results and participant behavior. Accordingly, whether KT prompts are presented orally or in writing should be treated as a deliberate study design choice, standardized within studies, and clearly reported.

Due to the evolution and advancement of cloud technology, intelligent cloud systems using big data and artificial intelligence built on scalable structure are available. The shift from conventional cloud architectures to intelligent self-optimizing architectures with real-time decision making capabilities is examined in this chapter. The cloud infrastructures of today do have weaknesses in terms of resource management, faulty security holes and a lack of backing for complex financial data. This chapter proposes a unified conceptual framework for AI-based analytics and smart cloud systems to combat these challenges. The platform boosts scalability, resource efficiency, and security via automated integration, distributed computing, and machine learning. To gain a holistic insight into the architecture, a detailed description of edge cloud integration, intelligent data processing layers and adaptive service management is provided.

“Active learning” has become a frequently invoked phrase in higher education discourse, yet it is a loose term spanning many, varied teaching and learning activities. It signals innovation, engagement and pedagogic progress, but also operates as a catch-all for anything that departs from the traditional lecture. Despite its conceptual vagueness, there is a growing sense that it is at the heart of an important shift in UK universities that confront mounting financial pressures, rising student numbers and the disruptive influence of Generative AI. In our most forward-thinking universities, active learning is moving from aspirational rhetoric into a central role in shaping the future of higher education teaching and learning.

Abstract With the rapid advancement of Generative AI (GenAI), debates have emerged about whether AI systems might replace human teachers in foreign language (FL) education. Using an adapted Technology Acceptance Model (TAM and TAM2) tailored to scientists, this study investigates the anticipated role of GenAI in FL education and scientists’ willingness to advocate its adoption. Based on questionnaire responses from 161 bilingual or multilingual GenAI scientists, the mixed‐methods study found that GenAI is generally perceived as useful and acceptable for FL education, but not as a replacement for teachers. They envision a future in which GenAI augments instruction while educators shift toward roles involving mentorship, cultural mediation, and ethical oversight. The findings suggest that GenAI adoption requires a human‐centered approach prioritizing output quality, trust, responsible use, and professional development, emphasizing augmentation over automation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping organizational decision-making, workforce management, and performance evaluation, creating both opportunities and challenges for contemporary leadership. Although organizations increasingly adopt AI to improve productivity, operational efficiency, and strategic decision-making, its implications for employee well-being and human-centered leadership remain complex and context dependent. This article develops an integrative conceptual analysis of how organizational leaders can introduce AI while supporting employee psychological well-being, strengthening organizational effectiveness, and maintaining ethical accountability. Drawing on foundational scholarship on AI adoption, algorithmic management, job demands and resources, self-determination, psychological safety, and AI governance, the article proposes a Human-Centered AI Leadership Integration Framework. The framework links four domains: AI and work design; leadership governance and employee participation; employee experience and well-being; and multidimensional, sustainable performance. The synthesis identifies plausible pathways through which AI may support workload management, information access, decision quality, and employee development, while also highlighting risks associated with algorithmic bias, intrusive surveillance, work intensification, job insecurity, and reduced autonomy. Because this is a conceptual review based on purposively selected sources, the framework is not presented as empirically validated and no causal effects are claimed. The article offers practical guidance for responsible implementation and sets out propositions and research priorities for future empirical investigation.

Generative AI in education is usually judged by the output of human-AI teams. That focus overlooks a second outcome: what people can still understand, challenge, repair, and adapt when assistance changes or disappears. We call this tension the generative paradox and distinguish four manifestations: performance, assistance, ownership, and capability stock. We propose developmental function allocation, which complements operational function allocation and meaningful human control by treating retained human capability as a design objective alongside current joint performance. The Anti-Prompt paradigm reverses the default interaction order: when immediate generation would preempt a consequential human act, AI should first create the conditions for human construction. We distinguish the validity of a product, responsibility for its construction, and evidence of capability after support changes. Representative Anti-Prompts, a canonical interaction sequence, and stress tests spanning mathematical reasoning, experimental science, software diagnosis, and lesson design make these distinctions concrete. We conclude with falsifiable predictions about retained capability and a system-level hypothesis about the reproduction and distribution of expertise.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: A current challenge in higher education policy is creating a transparent learning environment where students can disclose their use of GenAI to their faculty without any repercussions. This quantitative study investigates how self-reported GenAI usage patterns, course policies, and wrongful accusations shape student disclosure behaviors. Analyzing survey data from 560 students at four Northeastern U.S. institutions, the research explores disclosure through a trust-distrust lens. Results indicate that frequent GenAI users were significantly more likely to rarely disclose usage. Furthermore, participants who “always” disclosed their AI use faced over three times the odds of being accused by instructors than those who “never” disclosed. These findings highlight the hidden costs of transparency and underscore the need for equitable GenAI policies and trust-sensitive pedagogical practices. Ultimately, the study offers timely implications for developing supportive, AI-integrated learning environments that encourage transparency without the risk of repercussions
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Power systems are being instrumented at unprecedented density through supervisory control and data acquisition (SCADA), phasor measurement units (PMUs), advanced metering infrastructure, intelligent electronic devices, inverter telemetry, and digital twin platforms. This digitalization is increasingly important for integrating renewable generation, inverter-based resources, distributed energy resources (DERs), storage, electric vehicles, and flexible demand into sustainable low-carbon grids. Yet, greater visibility does not automatically produce better situational awareness or stronger control. We define illusory observability as a condition in which a power system appears increasingly visible but becomes less knowable, less trusted, or less governable when rapid intervention is required. Unlike situational awareness, bad-data detection, state estimation uncertainty, or classical controllability, the concept captures failures across the full measurement-to-intervention chain: sensing, inference, decision, authority, and actuation. These failures are amplified in renewable-rich and DER-intensive systems by fast software-defined dynamics, heterogeneous ownership, communication latency, cyber- and data integrity risks, cognitive overload, and fragmented control rights. We introduce a layered framework of physical observability, informational observability, and institutional controllability and show how misalignment among these layers can make visible low-carbon flexibility operationally unavailable. The article outlines a research and practice agenda focused on end-to-end latency and trust metrics, uncertainty-aware analytics, human-centered interfaces, verifiable telemetry, constrained digital twins, and preauthorized control pathways for distributed resources. Additional sensing remains essential, but its value should be judged by whether it enables timely, trusted, and authorized action. Therefore, closing the observability–controllability gap is a prerequisite for reliable renewable integration and sustainable power system operation.

Smart cities increasingly depend on digital technologies to manage urban services, use resources efficiently, and respond to the changing needs of citizens. Artificial intelligence (AI) can help city authorities analyse complex information, predict future conditions, and make informed decisions. However, the success of AI-based systems depends on more than their analytical capabilities. They also require reliable data from the Internet of Things (IoT) and governance practices that ensure transparency, accountability, and responsible use of technology. This paper examines how AI applications may influence smart decision-making in smart cities, with particular attention to the mediating roles of IoT integration and smart governance. Recent research published between 2024 and 2026 is reviewed to understand developments in AI-enabled urban services, connected infrastructure, and responsible digital governance. Based on this review, an integrated conceptual framework is proposed to explain the relationships among AI applications, IoT integration, smart governance, and decision-making outcomes. The framework considers decision accuracy, responsiveness, transparency, and resource efficiency as important dimensions of effective urban decision-making. It also highlights challenges related to data quality, privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, and public trust. Eight research hypotheses and a quantitative research methodology are proposed for future empirical investigation. The paper contributes a structured basis for examining how technological capabilities and governance arrangements may work together to support better urban decisions. The proposed relationships require validation through data collection and statistical analysis

The rapid uptake of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has changed the way work is carried out in organizations, bringing with it together new opportunity and new challenges for employee engagement. This approach looks at the effects of the approval of digital technology on employee engagement, with an exact focus on the organization's use of AI, the application of AI in sustainable Human Resource Management (HRM), employee trust and how often GenAI is used. In order to carry out the study, a qualitative multiple-case study method is used, based on four studies that had been published earlier and which were carried out in different organizational settings. The results show that AI adoption leads to superior levels of employee engagement if the technologies provide clear benefits related to employees' work, are compatible with the organization's current processes, and are properly supported by top management. By helping employees develop their skills, motivate them and grant them with opportunities to contribute, sustainable HRM practices implemented with AI can also help to further increase employee engagement. Trust among employees is also identified as a critical factor; as positive attitudes to AI are connected to superior levels of organizational commitment, which is positively related to employee engagement. Furthermore, while larger usage of GenAI does not necessarily correlate with greater job satisfaction, there is several evidences to propose that an increase in usage can lead to increased work engagement. The study findings indicate that the acceptance of digital technology is more than just about the technology being available: it relies on the responsible deployment, on the training of employees, on the enhancement of digital literacy, on the transparency of communication and on the support and engagement of leadership. Overall, the results emphasize the significance of a multi-faceted approach, encompassing both technological innovation and employee well-being and sustainable HRM practices, to foster authentic employee engagement and ensure the long-term effectiveness of the organization.

The bunkering of vessel is mandatory and technologically complex stage of organization of maritime transportation, associated with high level of occupational health risk for the crew members of both receiving and bunkering vessels. During bunkering operations, at sampling ship fuel, as well as work inside fuel tanks, the crew is exposed to complex impact of toxic vapors and aerosols of petroleum products. This exposure can result in development of acute pathological states and formation of chronic occupational diseases affecting respiratory, nervous, cardiovascular systems as well as haematopoiesis organs.In order to elaborate recommendations to decrease negative health aftermaths for health of crew members under bunkering operations, comprehensive analysis of organizational technological aspects of bunkering was carried out. It permitted to identify key irregularities regarding the stated subject and to formulate recommendations for their elimination.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Background: Musculoskeletal pain is a growing public health concern among school-aged children, with significant physical and psychosocial implications. Schoolbag weight and carrying style have been identified as critical ergonomic risk factors. However, evidence from developing countries, including Libya, remains limited, particularly regarding longitudinal impacts. Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the association between schoolbag weight, carrying style, and musculoskeletal pain over a five-year period among elementary schoolchildren in Misrata, Libya. Methods: A cohort of 443 elementary schoolchildren (grades 1-4) was followed for five years, with 421 completing all assessments. Data were collected on schoolbag weight, carrying style, walking duration, and pain characteristics. Descriptive statistics, Chi-square tests, and logistic regression were applied to explore the prevalence and predictors of pain. Repeated Measures ANOVA and Friedman tests were used to assess changes in continuous and categorical outcomes across time points. Results: Musculoskeletal pain prevalence increased from 0.0% at baseline to 10.1% at the first follow-up before declining to 5.6% and 6.2% in subsequent follow-ups. Carrying style emerged as the most significant predictor of pain, with the mid-back (T12) style reducing the risk of pain by up to 98.8% compared to the low-back (L3) style. Schoolbag weight, while exceeding recommended thresholds, was not a significant predictor of pain. Gender differences were noted, with girls at higher risk during early follow-ups. Walking duration played a marginal role, influencing pain risk only in the first follow-up. Conclusion: This study highlights the critical role of ergonomic carrying styles, particularly the mid-back (T12) position, in reducing musculoskeletal pain among schoolchildren. Findings challenge the conventional emphasis on bag weight alone and highlight the need for multifaceted interventions, including ergonomic education and policy changes, to promote musculoskeletal health.

This study aims to empirically investigate the structural pathways through which organizational factors associated with the adoption environment of generative artificial intelligence (AI) influence employees' intentions to adopt AI through psychological mechanisms.Based on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework, a macro-level technology adoption model, the adoption environment was categorized into technological, organizational, and environmental factors.AI self-efficacy and AI anxiety were established as mediating variables representing opposing psychological mechanisms, while intention to adopt was specified as the dependent variable.To empirically test the proposed research model, a survey was conducted among 327 Korean employees who were currently using generative AI in their work.The hypotheses were tested using structural equation modeling (SEM) and bootstrapping analysis.The results indicate that both technological and organizational factors significantly enhanced AI self-efficacy while simultaneously reducing AI anxiety.Environmental factors had a significant positive effect on AI self-efficacy but did not have a significant effect on reducing AI anxiety.Furthermore, AI self-efficacy was found to have a positive effect on intention to adopt, whereas AI anxiety was identified as a key mediating factor that negatively affects intention to adopt.This study contributes to the literature by identifying an integrated mechanism through which macro-level environmental stimuli are translated into behavioral intentions through individuals' internal psychological evaluations.From a practical perspective, the findings suggest that organizations should move beyond simply following external trends in generative AI adoption.Instead, they should focus on enhancing employees' self-efficacy through technological maturity and internal organizational training, while simultaneously addressing employees' concerns and fears regarding potential technological replacement.

This chapter establishes why cybersecurity is now a core business leadership responsibility rather than a purely technical function. It examines the fundamental drivers behind escalating cyber risk, including human behavior, rapid technological advancement, imperfect software design, artificial intelligence, geopolitical instability, and the commoditization of digital capability. The chapter explains why traditional technology-centric approaches to cybersecurity frequently fail and why business alignment, governance, resilience, and executive engagement are critical to success. The discussion highlights the economic realities of cybersecurity, including the impossibility of achieving perfect protection, the limitations of compliance-based thinking, and the operational challenges of defending organizations in a continuous 24/7 threat environment. It also explores how security, safety, and trust increasingly influence customer value propositions and competitive differentiation. The chapter concludes by presenting a strategic vision for cybersecurity that integrates business objectives, organizational resilience, risk management, and leadership accountability into a practical executive framework for decision-making in the age of AI.

This study examines the influence of the artistic and pedagogical legacy of Nikolai Mikhailovich Suetin – chief artist of the Leningrad Porcelain Factory – on the work of the factory’s sculptors and artists.The stylistic impact of N. M. Suetin's supremacist works on the individual creativity of the factory's artists is traced on a specific material, and the phenomenon of the art laboratory, which he directed, is revealed. The work of his students and colleagues contemporary to N. M. Suetin is highlighted, as well as the legacy of his ideas, which continued to live in the artistic porcelain of the LFZ of the second half of the 20th century. When considering the products of the LFZ, the models of artistic porcelain were mainly selected, which are subject to further mass replication. The choice of mass–produced objects is determined by the basic principles of creating artistic porcelain, developed by N. M.
